reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: This chapter describes the LRFD framework as applied to drilled shaft design. The basic LRFD equation requires that factored loads not exceed factored resistances, with factors calibrated to achieve target reliability. The general equation is: sum(eta_i * gamma_i * Q_i) <= phi * R_n, where eta_i is load modifier, gamma_i is load factor, Q_i is load effect, phi is resistance factor, and R_n is nominal resistance.
key_points: LRFD replaces ASD by using statistically calibrated load and resistance factors
Target reliability index beta = 3.0 for single drilled shafts (redundant) or beta = 3.5 (non-redundant)
Resistance factors are calibrated to AASHTO LRFD Bridge Design Specifications
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft designs using LRFD methodology

sections.title: Limit States and Load Combinations
sections.body: Drilled shaft design must satisfy Strength, Service, and Extreme Event limit states. Strength I is the primary limit state for axial and lateral resistance under gravity and live loads. Service I governs settlement and lateral deflection. Extreme Event I addresses seismic loading and Extreme Event II covers vessel collision and scour.
key_points: Strength I: gravity loads with load factors (DC=1.25, LL=1.75)
Service I: settlement and deflection checks at unfactored loads
Extreme Event I: seismic (gamma_EQ = 0.0 to 1.0)
Extreme Event II: vessel collision, vehicle collision, ice loads
Load modifier eta accounts for ductility, redundancy, and importance

sections.title: Geotechnical Strength Limit State
sections.body: Geotechnical resistance factors for drilled shafts are specified in AASHTO Table 10.5.5.2.4-1 and depend on the design method, soil type, and construction quality control measures. Higher resistance factors are permitted when static load tests are used for verification. The resistance factor for combined side and base resistance uses a weighted average based on relative contributions.
key_points: Alpha method in cohesive soil: phi = 0.45 (no load test), phi = 0.60 (with load test)
Beta method in cohesionless soil: phi = 0.55 (no load test), phi = 0.70 (with load test)
Rock socket side resistance: phi = 0.55 (no load test), phi = 0.70 (with load test)
Base resistance in cohesionless soil: phi = 0.50
Base resistance in cohesive soil: phi = 0.40
Base resistance on rock (CGS method): phi = 0.50
Static load test verification allows significant increase in resistance factors
Uplift resistance factors are lower than compression factors

sections.title: Structural Strength Limit State
sections.body: Structural design of drilled shafts follows reinforced concrete design per AASHTO LRFD. The structural resistance factor phi = 0.75 for axial compression and phi = 0.90 for flexure. Combined axial and flexural loading is evaluated using P-M interaction diagrams. Minimum reinforcement is 1% of gross cross-sectional area for shafts designed for lateral loading.
key_points: phi = 0.75 for axial compression (spiral confined)
phi = 0.90 for flexure
Minimum 1% longitudinal steel for laterally loaded shafts
Maximum reinforcement limited by constructability (cage must allow concrete flow)
P-M interaction diagram governs combined loading

sections.title: Service Limit State
sections.body: Service limit state design ensures that settlement and lateral deflection remain within tolerable limits. Tolerable settlement for bridge foundations is typically 1 inch for simple spans and 1/2 inch for continuous spans. Analytical methods for computing settlement include t-z curve methods, elastic continuum solutions, and simplified closed-form expressions. Resistance factors for service limit state are typically 1.0.
key_points: Settlement limits: typically 1 inch (simple spans) or 0.5 inch (continuous spans)
Lateral deflection limits depend on structural requirements and p-y analysis
Resistance factor for service limit state = 1.0
Group settlement may be significantly larger than single shaft settlement
Service limit state often controls design for large-diameter shafts
sections.applicability: Settlement and deflection checks for drilled shaft foundations

sections.title: Extreme Event Limit State
sections.body: Extreme event limit states address infrequent but severe loading including seismic events, vessel collision, and scour. Resistance factors for extreme events are typically 1.0 for geotechnical resistance. Scour is treated as a change in geometry (not a load) by removing soil to the design scour depth. Seismic design requires evaluation of liquefaction potential and kinematic loading from lateral spreading.
key_points: Resistance factor phi = 1.0 for extreme event limit states
Scour removes soil to design scour depth; check flood not combined with seismic
Seismic loading includes inertial forces from superstructure and kinematic effects
Vessel collision evaluated under Extreme Event II
Liquefaction potential must be evaluated for seismic events

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: LRFD design for drilled shafts requires satisfaction of strength, service, and extreme event limit states. Resistance factors from AASHTO are calibrated to achieve target reliability and are method-specific. Static load testing provides the most reliable basis for resistance factor calibration and justifies higher resistance factors.
key_points: Table 10-5 resistance factors are central to drilled shaft LRFD design
Load testing significantly improves design economy through higher resistance factors
Service limit state (settlement) often controls design for large shafts
sections.applicability: Summary of LRFD framework for drilled shaft design
